stimulus.text:
Aircraft carriers lost at two Pacific naval battles in 1942.

| Battle | Date | Japanese carriers lost | American carriers lost |
| Coral Sea | May 1942 | 1 | 1 |
| Midway | June 1942 | 4 | 1 |
stimulus.source_note: Figures from 5 Steps Chapter 24 (Midway: Japan lost four aircraft carriers and over 200 planes; the United States lost one carrier) and Barron's Chapter 9 (Coral Sea: the U.S. Navy stopped a Japanese fleet headed to New Guinea).

source: original; stimulus drawn from book-grounded figures and paraphrases (see source_note)
stem: The Battle of the Coral Sea, fought in May 1942, was unusual for a naval battle. What made it different?

options.text: It was fought entirely by submarines
options.misconception: The battle was fought by carrier aircraft, not by submarines.

options.text: No American ships took part in the fighting
options.misconception: American carriers took part; the Lexington was lost in the battle.

options.text: It was the first battle in which Japan ever lost a warship at sea
options.misconception: Japan had lost ships before Coral Sea, including in earlier Pacific fighting.

options.text: The opposing ships never saw each other; the fighting was done by carrier aircraft

rationales.A: Carrier aircraft did the fighting, not submarines.
rationales.B: American carriers fought there, and the Lexington was lost.
rationales.C: Japan had lost ships in earlier fighting; Coral Sea was new for another reason.
rationales.D: The ships never saw each other; carrier aircraft did all the fighting.
rationales.general:
1. Background from the books: Coral Sea was the first major naval battle in which the ships never saw each other.
2. All the fighting was carried out by aircraft flying from carriers.
3. The battle stopped a Japanese fleet headed for New Guinea.
4. It set the pattern for Midway a month later, where carriers again decided the battle.
Remember: a first in warfare often names a new technology, so look for what the ships did not do.
